steps.observation: Work on this for 30 seconds; do not stop early. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Conceptually, a transformer is built around one core idea: instead of processing a sequence step-by-step (like a recurrent network), it lets every element in the sequence look at every other element in parallel and decide who matters. This is done through “self-attention.”

Here’s the key chain of ideas in plain language:

1. Tokens as vectors  
   • Every word, sub-word, or character you feed in is first turned into a vector (an embedding).  
   • Add a “positional encoding” to each vector so the model knows where a token sits in the sentence (because, unlike RNNs, transformers have no built-in notion of order).

2. Self-attention: learning who to listen to  
   • For every token, the network forms three little projections of its embedding: a Query, a Key, and a Value.  
   • To decide how much one token should pay attention to another, you take that token’s Query and dot-product it with the other token’s Key. A high dot product means “this other token is relevant to me.”  
   • Normalize all those dot products with softmax so they add up to 1. Those become attention weights.  
   • Use those weights to blend the corresponding Value vectors. The result is a new representation of the token, informed by the entire context.

3. Multi-head attention: seeing relationships in multiple “views”  
   • Instead of doing self-attention once, the model does it many times in parallel, each time with its own learned Q/K/V projections (“heads”).  
   • Each head can specialize—one might focus on subject–verb agreement, another on coreference, another on local syntax, etc.  
   • Concatenate the heads’ results, run them through a small linear layer, and you’ve now captured many relational patterns at once.

4. Feed-forward sublayer: reasoning token-by-token  
   • After attention, each token’s context-mixed vector goes through a small two-layer fully-connected network with an activation (usually GELU or ReLU).  
   • This lets the model perform more complex non-linear transformations individually on each token.

5. Residual connections and layer normalization: stability and depth  
   • The output of each sublayer (attention, then feed-forward) is added back to its input (a residual skip) and normalized.  
   • Skip connections help gradients flow through very deep stacks (dozens or even hundreds of layers) without vanishing or exploding.

6. Stacking layers for richer representations  
   • A single layer gives every token a context-aware representation. Stacking many layers means each token can iteratively refine its understanding, compounding simple relationships into higher-level abstractions (syntax → phrases → semantics → world knowledge).

7. Encoder, decoder, or both  
   • In an encoder-only transformer (e.g., BERT), you keep stacking layers that look at the full input.  
   • In a decoder-only transformer (e.g., GPT), each token can only attend to earlier tokens (via masking) so it can be used for left-to-right generation.  
   • In sequence-to-sequence models (e.g., original “Transformer” for translation), an encoder processes the input sentence, and a decoder attends both to its own past words and to the encoder’s outputs.

8. Training objective shapes the knowledge  
   • Masked-language-model objective (BERT): hide some tokens, predict them from context → good bidirectional understanding.  
   • Autoregressive objective (GPT): predict the next token given all previous tokens → good at fluent text generation.  
   • Other objectives (translation, summarization, code completion, multimodal tasks) all influence what information the transformer learns to encode.

Put together, the transformer is like a giant “message-passing” machine: every layer lets tokens broadcast information to and receive information from all others, repeatedly refining their meanings. Because this is parallelizable (matrix multiplications dominate), it trains much faster on modern hardware than RNNs and scales well to vast data and parameter counts—hence their success in language, vision, protein folding, and beyond.
